He is presumed to have died in the crash of a light aircraft in Alaska in October 1972; his body was never found. He was a member of the Democratic Party.

BG:B001323.tier_writeup: Nicholas Begich is a sitting House member who has voted against U.S. aid to Israel in 2025‑07‑18, but he has never broken with his party on that issue and has not shown a consistent anti‑Israel stance. His anti‑intervention votes are limited to a handful of foreign‑policy amendments and he has not signed any discharge petitions against leadership. He has cosponsored several hawkish Iran and Taiwan bills, indicating a willingness to support interventionist measures. He has no known Israel‑lobby contributions, but the lack of a consistent record on the anchor issue and the absence of a breaking vote on aid to Israel mean he does not meet the threshold for a reliable ally. He is therefore classified as a soft signal, not a dependable anti‑establishment ally.

BG:M001212.tier_writeup: Barry Moore presents a bifurcated record that fails the coalition's standards for a reliable anti-establishment ally. While he frequently breaks with party leadership to vote against military aid for Ukraine and NATO, he remains a staunch supporter of aid to the State of Israel, voting for multiple supplemental packages and against amendments to strike such funding. His record on the use of force is similarly interventionist; he has repeatedly voted against concurrent resolutions that would direct the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from foreign conflicts. Furthermore, his legislative activity includes sponsoring a resolution to condemn the International Criminal Court's actions against Israeli leadership and cosponsoring aggressive sanctions against Iran. This pattern suggests his anti-interventionism is selective and partisan rather than principled, particularly given his consistent support for military engagement and aid in the Middle East. As he is retiring, his record serves as a final confirmation of his establishment alignment on core interventionist pillars.
BG:M001212.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently supports military aid to Israel and votes against restraining the U.S. use of force abroad.

BG:F000481.tier_writeup: Shomari Figures is a sitting Democrat from Alabama who failed the anchor test by voting against amendments to cut aid to Israel in 2025 and 2026. His record on military aid to other countries is consistently interventionist, including votes to fund Ukraine and Taiwan. While he voted for the repeal of the 2002 AUMF, this was a party-line vote with 99% of his own party voting the same way, not a principled defection. He has zero breaking anti-interventionist votes against his own party leadership. Figures is heavily targeted by pro-Israel lobby money, with DMFI PAC spending $7 million to support his re-election. This financial dependence on the establishment foreign policy base contradicts any claim of anti-interventionist principle. His record shows he is a standard establishment Democrat who votes with his party on all major foreign policy issues.
BG:F000481.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted against cutting aid to Israel, received millions in pro-Israel super PAC support, and cast zero breaking votes against his own party.

BG:R000575.tier_screen: sponsors/cosponsors 16 arms, aid or war bills
BG:R000575.tier_writeup: Mike Rogers is a reliable establishment figure whose record is defined by consistent support for foreign intervention and military aid. On the anchor issue of aid to the State of Israel, Rogers has repeatedly voted for supplemental funding and against any measures to strike or prohibit such assistance. His record on the use of force is equally interventionist; he has voted against the repeal of the 1991 and 2002 war authorizations and has consistently opposed more than ten separate resolutions directing the removal of U.S. armed forces from foreign territories. While he has cast rare votes against specific aid packages for NATO or Ukraine, these are outliers in a career-long pattern of backing the military-industrial status quo. Furthermore, reports that his campaign staff includes registered agents for Israel reinforce his alignment with foreign interests over anti-interventionist principles. Rogers remains a firm part of the interventionist consensus in Congress.
BG:R000575.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is a consistent supporter of military aid to Israel and foreign military interventions, with a voting record that aligns almost entirely with the establishment.

BG:A000055.description: Robert Brown Aderholt is an American politician and attorney from Alabama. A socially conservative member of the Republican Party and a member of the Tea Party Caucus, he is currently serving as a U.S. representative, representing Alabama's 4th congressional district since 1997. The district includes most of Tuscaloosa County north of the Black Warrior River, as well as Birmingham's far northern suburbs in Walker County and the southern suburbs of Huntsville and Decatur.

BG:A000055.tier_screen: breaks from own party toward the anti side on 3 foreign-policy votes
BG:A000055.tier_writeup: Robert Aderholt is a long-serving Republican member of Congress with a record that is overwhelmingly interventionist. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he has consistently voted for supplemental security assistance (H R 7217, H R 8034, H R 8369) and voted against amendments to strike that funding (H R 4016, H R 8595). While he has cast a few breaking votes against his party on specific military aid amendments, such as cutting NATO funding (H R 4366) and opposing the Ukraine Support Act (H R 2913), these are outliers in a record of supporting arms to Taiwan (H R 1531) and rejecting various restrictions on aid to Ukraine and Lebanon. He consistently votes against restraining U.S. use of force and against repealing war authorizations (H R 3838, H CON RES 68, H CON RES 75). His rare anti-interventionist votes do not outweigh a career of supporting the establishment foreign policy consensus, and he has signed no discharge petitions to bypass leadership. His record indicates partisan alignment rather than anti-establishment principle.
BG:A000055.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for aid to Israel and generally supports interventionist military aid and use of force.

BG:P000609.tier_writeup: Gary Palmer is a sitting member of the House who consistently aligns with the establishment on the coalition's anchor issue. He has voted for multiple supplemental security assistance packages for Israel, including H R 7217, H R 8034, and H R 8369, and voted against an amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security (H R 4016). While he has cast several anti-interventionist votes regarding military aid to Ukraine and Lebanon, these are inconsistent and do not outweigh his support for the Israel lobby's priorities. His record on the use of force is overwhelmingly interventionist, having voted against numerous resolutions to remove U.S. forces from foreign soil (H CON RES 61, 64, 68, 84, 89, 93, 108). He also voted against repealing the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force (H R 3838). His occasional breaks from his party on Ukraine funding appear as isolated instances rather than a principled anti-interventionist shift. As a member of the Republican Policy Committee leadership, he is deeply embedded in the establishment structure.
BG:P000609.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel and opposes efforts to restrain U.S. force abroad.

BG:C001087.tier_writeup: Eric Crawford is a reliable establishment interventionist whose record shows consistent support for foreign military engagement. He fails the coalition's anchor test, having voted repeatedly for military aid to Israel, including H R 7217 and H R 8034. His record on the use of force is particularly hawkish; throughout 2025 and 2026, he voted against every resolution to remove U.S. armed forces from foreign territories, such as H CON RES 61 and H CON RES 93. Furthermore, he voted against repealing the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force (AUMF) in 2025. While he has cast a handful of votes against the transfer of cluster munitions, these are isolated defections in an otherwise interventionist career. He also supports military aid to Taiwan and Ukraine, further cementing his alignment with establishment foreign policy.
BG:C001087.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently supports military aid to Israel, opposes the removal of U.S. troops from foreign conflicts, and votes against repealing outdated war authorizations.

BG:H001072.tier_writeup: J. Hill is a sitting member of Congress with a record that is overwhelmingly interventionist. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, Hill has consistently voted for military assistance, including voting Yea on H R 7217, H R 8034, and H R 8369, and voting against an amendment to strike Israeli Cooperative Security funding in H R 4016. In other areas, Hill has cosponsored numerous arms and aid bills, including the Stand with Israel Act and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act. While Hill cast a few breaking votes, such as voting against the Ukraine Support Act (H R 2913) and for an amendment to strike NATO funding (H R 8580), these are isolated instances in a record of 76 focus votes where only 4 were anti-interventionist. Hill consistently votes against resolutions to remove U.S. forces from abroad and against restraining the use of force. The record shows a partisan alignment with establishment foreign policy rather than a principled anti-interventionist stance.
BG:H001072.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because they have consistently voted for military aid to Israel and generally support interventionist policies.

BG:W000809.tier_writeup: Steve Womack is a sitting member of Congress with a record that aligns closely with the foreign policy establishment. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he has consistently voted for military assistance, including voting Yea on H R 7217, H R 8034, and H R 8369. His record in other areas is similarly interventionist: he has voted against repealing war authorizations (H R 3838) and against removing U.S. forces from foreign soil (H CON RES 68, 84, 89, 108). While he cast a single breaking anti-interventionist vote against the Ukraine Support Act (H R 2913) on 2026-06-04, this is an isolated incident in a record of 74 focus votes. He has not signed any discharge petitions to bypass leadership on anti-interventionist measures. His support for the establishment is further evidenced by his public calls to support Israel and his approval of Benjamin Netanyahu's address to Congress.
BG:W000809.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel and generally supports interventionist foreign policy.

BG:W000821.tier_screen: breaks from own party toward the anti side on 8 foreign-policy votes
BG:W000821.tier_writeup: Bruce Westerman is a reliable establishment vote who fails the coalition's anchor test on aid to the State of Israel. He has consistently voted for supplemental security assistance and against amendments to strike funding for Israeli cooperative programs, while cosponsoring multiple resolutions of support for the state. His record on the use of force is overwhelmingly interventionist; between 2025 and 2026, he voted against at least nine separate resolutions that would have directed the removal of U.S. armed forces from various foreign theaters. While he has occasionally broken with party leadership to vote against Ukraine aid or to repeal the 1991 and 2002 Iraq war authorizations, these votes are inconsistent with his broader support for military assistance to Taiwan and his opposition to other troop withdrawal measures. His record suggests that his occasional anti-interventionist votes are isolated or partisan rather than part of a coherent non-interventionist principle. Ultimately, his commitment to maintaining U.S. military presence and aid flows abroad makes him an unreliable ally for the coalition.
BG:W000821.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently supports military aid to Israel and repeatedly votes against withdrawing U.S. troops from foreign conflicts.

BG:S001183.tier_writeup: David Schweikert's record is firmly establishment on the coalition's anchor issue, having consistently voted for military aid to Israel in 2024, 2025, and 2026. While he has occasionally broken with his party to support the repeal of the Iraq War authorizations and to limit U.S. involvement in Somalia and Syria, these votes are the exception rather than the rule. His overall anti-interventionist ratio is low at 14%, and he has recently voted against numerous resolutions to withdraw U.S. forces from foreign conflicts. Furthermore, his support for military aid to Taiwan and Ukraine in 2026 underscores a lack of consistent principle across the coalition's five areas. As a retiring member with a record that favors interventionist supplemental spending, he cannot be counted on as a reliable ally.
BG:S001183.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel and has an inconsistent record on war authorizations and use of force.

BG:C001132.tier_writeup: Elijah Crane is a sitting member of Congress with a record of breaking from his own party on foreign policy, but he fails the coalition's primary test. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he is inconsistent, voting against supplemental security assistance in February and April 2024 (H R 7217, H R 8034), but voting for the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 (H R 8369) and voting against an amendment to strike Israeli funding in July 2025 (H R 4016). While he has shown principled defiance by voting against military aid to Ukraine and NATO and supporting the repeal of the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, his record on the use of force abroad has been largely interventionist in 2026, voting against resolutions to remove U.S. forces (H CON RES 86, 84, 108, 89, 93). He has signed discharge petitions against his own leadership, and he has no recorded funding from the Israel lobby. However, the anchor rule requires consistency on Israel aid, which Crane lacks.
BG:C001132.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel.

BG:A000381.tier_writeup: Yassamin Ansari is a Democratic Representative from Arizona's 3rd district, formerly a Phoenix City Council member. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel she voted both against (2025-07-18) and for (2026-07-15) anti‑intervention measures, showing inconsistency. She has been consistently anti‑intervention on use‑of‑force resolutions (9 of 9) and war authorizations (3 of 3), but she voted interventionist on several military‑aid bills for Taiwan, Ukraine and other allies. She has two breaking anti‑intervention votes, but they were not against party leadership and her discharge‑petition signatures were all with her own party. No money from the Israel lobby is recorded, but she has not actively backed an establishment leader. Overall her record is mixed, with enough anti‑intervention votes to be a signal but insufficient consistency on the anchor issue or leadership defiance to be a reliable ally.
BG:A000381.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent and she has not shown strong defiance of party leadership.

BG:S001211.tier_writeup: Greg Stanton is a sitting Democrat from Arizona who has served in Congress since 2019. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, as he voted for supplemental security assistance in 2024 and voted against striking funding for Israeli Cooperative Security in 2025. While he has cast anti-interventionist votes on war authorizations and use of force, these votes largely align with his party's majority rather than representing a principled break from establishment policy. He has no breaking anti-interventionist votes on the anchor issue of aid to Israel. His cosponsorships include measures supporting the removal of forces from hostilities with Iran, but also include resolutions condemning Hamas, which reflects a mixed approach. The lack of consistency on the anchor issue disqualifies him from being counted as a reliable anti-establishment ally.
BG:S001211.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted for aid to Israel in 2024 and 2025, failing the anchor requirement for reliability.

He was president of the Arizona Senate from 2013 to 2017. Biggs served as chairman of the Freedom Caucus from 2019 to 2022.

BG:B001302.tier_screen: breaks from own party toward the anti side on 36 foreign-policy votes
BG:B001302.tier_writeup: Andy Biggs has a mixed record that fails the coalition's reliability test. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he is inconsistent, voting against supplemental security assistance in February and April 2024 (H R 7217, H R 8034), but voting for the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 (H R 8369) and voting against an amendment to strike Israeli funding in July 2025 (H R 4016). While he has a strong record of breaking with his party to oppose military aid to Ukraine and NATO, this is offset by recent interventionist votes on the use of force abroad, including voting against resolutions to remove U.S. forces in June and July 2026 (H CON RES 86, 84, 108, 89, 93). He has shown principle by breaking with his party on Yemen and certain arms deals, but his inconsistency on Israel and recent shift toward supporting the use of force abroad disqualify him. He has not signed any discharge petitions against leadership. His lack of lobby money is noted, but his voting record does not meet the floor for reliability.
BG:B001302.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel and has recently trended toward interventionist votes.

BG:G000565.tier_writeup: Paul Gosar has a mixed record that fails the coalition's reliability test. While he has frequently broken with his party to oppose military aid to Ukraine and other nations, he is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, voting for the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 and voting against an amendment to strike Israeli funding in July 2025. His record in other areas is similarly unstable; although he voted to repeal the Iraq War authorizations in 2025, he has consistently voted against resolutions to remove U.S. forces from abroad in 2026. Most concerning is his recent trajectory, where he voted for the Ukraine Support Act in June 2026 and rejected amendments to prohibit military aid in July 2026. While he has no recorded money from the Israel lobby, his voting pattern shows a lack of principled consistency. He does not meet the floor for a reliable ally because he wavers on the anchor and has recently reverted to establishment positions on use of force and military aid.
BG:G000565.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel and has recently trended toward interventionist votes.

BG:H001068.tier_writeup: Jared Huffman is a Democratic incumbent from California who has shown intermittent anti-interventionist signals but lacks the consistency required for a reliable ally. While he has voted against several authorizations for the use of force and has supported repealing certain war authorizations, his record on the anchor issue—aid to the State of Israel—is inconsistent, having voted both for and against such assistance. He has also demonstrated inconsistency regarding military aid to other countries, such as voting against amendments to prohibit funding for Ukraine or Taiwan. Although he has broken with his party on specific use-of-force resolutions, these votes do not constitute a sustained pattern of defiance against the establishment. He has signed several discharge petitions, but these were not directed against his own party leadership. Without a consistent record of opposing military aid to Israel and a more stable stance on global arms transfers, he remains a soft signal rather than a hard ally.
BG:H001068.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent and he has not demonstrated a sustained, principled break from his party on military assistance.

BG:T000460.description: Charles Michael Thompson is an American politician serving as the U.S. representative for California's 4th congressional district since 1999. The district, in the northern portion of the San Francisco Bay Area, includes all of Lake and Napa counties and parts of Solano, Yolo and Sonoma counties. He is a moderate Democrat and member of the conservative Blue Dog Coalition. Thompson was first elected in 1998, winning reelection 13 times, before losing his seat in 2026 to liberal challenger Eric Jones 52.5% to 47.5% in an upset.

He has not demonstrated the required principle of breaking with his party on major foreign policy escalations, as most of his anti-interventionist votes align with his party majority. Furthermore, he has not signed any discharge petitions to bypass party leadership on these issues. His voting pattern suggests he follows the establishment line on most high-stakes military and aid decisions.

BG:M001177.tier_writeup: Tom McClintock is a sitting Republican member of Congress with a record that fails the coalition's primary test. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he has consistently voted the interventionist side, including voting for supplemental security assistance in February 2024 (H R 7217), military appropriations in April 2024 (H R 8034), and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 (H R 8369), while voting against an amendment to strike Israeli Cooperative funding in July 2025 (H R 4016). While he has cast several breaking votes against his own party on other issues, such as repealing war authorizations (H R 256, H R 3838) and opposing some aid to Ukraine and NATO, these are inconsistent and do not outweigh his support for the anchor. His recent record shows a trend toward interventionist votes on the use of force and military aid, including supporting the PROTECT Taiwan Act in February 2026 (H R 1531). Because he has never voted the anti-interventionist side on aid to Israel, he cannot be considered a reliable ally.
BG:M001177.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to the State of Israel.

BG:G000559.tier_writeup: John Garamendi is a long-serving Democratic incumbent from California. While he has demonstrated some anti-interventionist tendencies, specifically regarding war authorizations and the use of force, his record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent. He has voted against several supplemental security assistance bills for Israel, but he also voted in favor of the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 and failed to vote against the Greene amendment to strike Israeli Cooperative funding in July 2025. His record on military aid to other countries is also mixed, frequently voting against amendments to prohibit funding for Ukraine, Taiwan, and Lebanon. He has broken with his party on several occasions, including votes to repeal war authorizations and to direct the removal of troops from unauthorized hostilities. However, because he has not held a consistent anti-Israel aid position and has not signed discharge petitions to bypass party leadership, he remains in the establishment category.

BG:H001090.description: Joshua Keck Harder is an American politician who has served as the U.S. representative for California's 9th congressional district since 2023, after representing the 10th district from 2019 to 2023. A member of the Democratic Party, he was first elected in 2018 by defeating Republican incumbent Jeff Denham. After the 2020 redistricting, he won reelection in the newly drawn 9th district, which covers the majority of San Joaquin County and includes Stockton, Tracy, Lodi, and Manteca.

BG:H001090.tier_writeup: Josh Harder is a sitting Democrat from California who serves on the Appropriations Committee and is a vice chair of the New Democrat Coalition. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with three anti-interventionist votes and two interventionist votes, including a Yea vote on H R 8034 in 2024 and a Nay vote on the Greene amendment in 2025. While he cast a breaking vote in 2025 to repeal the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, this single defection is insufficient to overcome the inconsistency on the Israel anchor. He has signed multiple discharge petitions, but the facts indicate zero applicable discharge petitions were signed, suggesting these may have been procedural or non-interventionist in nature. His voting record on military aid to other countries is largely interventionist, with only two anti votes out of thirty, including a Yea vote on the PROTECT Taiwan Act and the Ukraine Support Act. Although he has no tracked money from the Israel lobby and was targeted by AIPAC for his anti-aid votes, the lack of consistency on the primary issue prevents him from being classified as a reliable ally. His positions appear mixed, with some principled stands on war powers but significant alignment with the establishment on broader foreign aid and military support. He is unlikely to hold under pressure on the specific issue of Israel aid given his prior interventionist votes in that area.
BG:H001090.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on aid to Israel is inconsistent, failing the anchor requirement for reliability.

His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with 4 of 5 votes anti-interventionist, including a critical 'Nay' on the 2024 supplemental aid bill (H R 8034) where only 17% of his party voted the same way. He has signed multiple discharge petitions, including those to repeal the 2002 AUMF, demonstrating a willingness to break with party leadership on procedural grounds. His financial record shows no tracked money from the Israel lobby, which is a positive signal, but the voting record remains the primary determinant. The combination of a strong anti-war stance on other issues but a failure to hold the line on Israel aid suggests a mixed record that does not meet the threshold for a 'hard' ally.

BG:L000607.tier_writeup: Sam Liccardo is a sitting Democrat from California who previously served as Mayor of San Jose. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is interventionist, as he voted Nay on the Greene amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security in July 2025 and again on an amendment to prohibit funds from being used for Israel in July 2026. He has zero breaking anti-interventionist votes, meaning he has never voted against the majority of his own party to block interventionist measures. While he has voted for some non-binding resolutions directing the removal of forces from Iran and Venezuela, these votes were taken with 97-100% of his own party, indicating party-line voting rather than principled defiance. He also voted Yea on the PROTECT Taiwan Act and the Ukraine Support Act, further demonstrating a willingness to support military aid to other countries. His cosponsorship of the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act and his vote for sanctions on foreign entities confirm an interventionist stance on sanctions. There is no evidence of him signing discharge petitions to bypass his party leadership on these issues. His record is consistent with a standard establishment Democrat who votes with his party on foreign policy, regardless of the specific interventionist nature of the bills.
BG:L000607.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted the interventionist side on the anchor issue of aid to Israel and has no breaking votes against his own party on any interventionist measure.

BG:K000389.description: Rohit Khanna is an American politician and attorney serving as the U.S. representative from California's 17th congressional district since 2017. A member of the Democratic Party, he defeated eight-term incumbent Democratic representative Mike Honda in the 2016 general election, after first running for the same seat in 2014. Khanna also served as the deputy assistant secretary in the United States Department of Commerce under President Barack Obama from 2009 to 2011.

BG:K000389.tier_writeup: Ro Khanna is a sitting House member who has voted against U.S. aid to Israel in three of four relevant roll‑calls, but he also voted for aid in one instance, breaking the anchor rule that defines a reliable anti‑interventionist. In the other four policy areas—military aid to other countries, sanctions, use of force abroad, and war authorizations—his record is mixed, with both anti‑ and interventionist votes. He has made several breaking anti‑votes and has cosponsored numerous anti‑war and anti‑aid resolutions, indicating some principled positions, yet his inconsistent stance on Israel and the lack of a clear, sustained pattern of defiance against his party’s leadership reduce confidence. No evidence shows he actively backs an establishment leader, and his campaign finance data are unavailable, so we cannot rule out political posturing. Overall, his record does not meet the strict criteria for a hard ally, but he is not a pure establishment figure either, placing him in the soft category.
BG:K000389.tier_bottom_line: Does not count: the bridge from the 118th Congress ended when they voted for aid to Israel on 2025-07-18 (H R 4016).

BG:L000397.tier_writeup: Zoe Lofgren is a long-serving Democrat from California who has been in Congress since 1995. Her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with three anti-interventionist votes and two interventionist votes. Specifically, she voted for the supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel in April 2024 and voted against an amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security in July 2025. While she has voted against other forms of aid and has signed discharge petitions, the inconsistency on the anchor issue disqualifies her from being a reliable ally. Her votes on military aid to other countries are consistently interventionist, as she voted against amendments to prohibit aid to Ukraine, Lebanon, and Taiwan. She has voted against repealing war authorizations and has not broken with her party on the most critical interventionist votes. Her record shows a pattern of supporting broad defense spending and military aid packages, which aligns with the establishment rather than an anti-interventionist principle.
BG:L000397.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, failing to meet the reliability floor for a sitting member.

His record on aid to Israel is inconsistent and interventionist, as he voted Yea on H R 7217 in 2024 and Nay on the Greene amendment to strike Israeli funding in 2025. In the area of military aid to other countries, he has consistently voted against restrictions on aid to Ukraine and other nations, such as voting Nay on amendments to prohibit funding for Ukraine in 2024 and 2025. He voted Yea on the Ukraine Support Act in 2026, further demonstrating his support for interventionist policies. On sanctions, he voted Yea on H R 1998 in 2025, imposing sanctions on foreign entities, which is an interventionist stance. Regarding the use of force abroad, he has voted Yea on several concurrent resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces, but these votes were largely party-line and did not constitute breaking votes against his own party's leadership. He voted Yea on the repeal of the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force in 2025, which is an anti-interventionist vote, but this was part of a broader party consensus. Costa has no breaking anti-interventionist votes on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, and his record shows a pattern of supporting military aid and sanctions. His cosponsorship of the Ukraine Support Act and other pro-intervention bills further undermines any claim of anti-establishment alignment. The record does not support a verdict of hard or soft, as he fails the anchor test and shows consistent interventionist behavior in other areas.

BG:O000019.tier_writeup: Jay Obernolte is a Republican representative from California. While he has cast four breaking votes against his own party on anti-interventionist measures—including repealing the 2002 AUMF (H R 256) and the 1991/2002 AUMFs (H R 3838)—these are outweighed by a broad record of supporting military aid and force. He has voted for military assistance to Taiwan (H R 1531) and consistently voted against resolutions to remove U.S. forces from Syria and other locations (H CON RES 61, 64, 68, 84, 89, 93, 108). He also cosponsored sanctions against Iran (H R 1422). His occasional defections on war authorizations do not establish a reliable anti-establishment pattern given his adherence to the party line on Israel and general military aid.
BG:O000019.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel and lacks a principled anti-interventionist record.

BG:R000599.tier_screen: marked anti on the focus issue by votes or statements
BG:R000599.tier_writeup: Raul Ruiz (D-CA) is a sitting member whose record shows a significant but inconsistent anti-interventionist stance. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he is inconsistent, having voted against supplemental security assistance in 2024 but voting for the supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel in April 2024 and again in July 2026. This failure to hold the line on the anchor issue disqualifies him from being a reliable ally, as the coalition requires consistency on this specific front. While he has cast breaking votes against his own party on military aid to other countries, such as amendments to cut NATO funding or prohibit cluster munitions, his record on Ukraine aid is also inconsistent, voting for the Ukraine Support Act in 2026 after previously voting against amendments to restrict aid. He has voted consistently against broad war authorizations and for resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces from various conflicts, which are strong anti-interventionist signals. However, his recent votes for military aid to Israel and Ukraine contradict his earlier principled stands, suggesting that his anti-interventionism is selective or subject to political pressure. There is no evidence of him signing discharge petitions against his own leadership, and while he has no tracked money from the Israel lobby, his voting record on the anchor issue is the primary barrier to reliability.
BG:R000599.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he failed to hold the anti-interventionist line on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, voting for supplemental military aid in 2024 and 2026 despite earlier opposition.

She has signed no discharge petitions that defy her own leadership. She also cosponsored the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act (HR 1422) and the PROTECT Taiwan Act (HR 1531) and Ukraine Support Act (HR 2913), all interventionist military-aid bills. TrackAIPAC records show no direct contributions, but press reports confirm she joined an AIPAC-funded congressional trip to Israel in August 2025. Her first anti vote came nine months into her term, and she has not held a consistent anti line on the anchor issue. The pattern is partisan alignment, not principled anti-interventionism.

BG:L000582.tier_writeup: Ted Lieu is a sitting Democrat from California who has served in Congress since 2019. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent and ultimately interventionist, as he voted Yea on H.R. 7217 in February 2024 to provide supplemental security assistance to Israel and voted Nay on the Greene amendment in July 2025 to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security. Although he voted Nay on the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024, his subsequent votes for aid demonstrate that he does not hold a consistent anti-interventionist line on the state of Israel. In the area of military aid to other countries, he has consistently voted with his party to provide assistance to Ukraine, Taiwan, and Lebanon, rejecting amendments that would have prohibited such funding. On sanctions, his record is mixed, with votes against the No U.S. Financing for Iran Act but in favor of other sanctions bills. He has voted against broad war authorizations and in favor of resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities, which aligns with anti-interventionist principles in those specific instances. However, his failure to maintain an anti-interventionist stance on Israel aid, combined with his consistent support for military aid to other countries, indicates he is not a reliable ally for the coalition. His voting record suggests he prioritizes party alignment and broader geopolitical interests over a strict anti-interventionist framework.
BG:L000582.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted for Israel military aid in 2024 and 2025, failing the anchor requirement for reliability.

BG:K000400.tier_writeup: Sydney Kamlager-Dove is a sitting Democratic Representative from California. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel she has been inconsistent, voting anti in 2024-02-06 and 2024-05-16 but voting for a supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid on 2024-04-15 and again supporting an amendment to prohibit funding for Israeli cooperative projects in 2025-07-18, showing a mixed record. Her broader anti‑intervention record shows some consistency on war authorizations and use‑of‑force resolutions (all anti), but she is mixed on military aid to other countries (anti on a few amendments but interventionist on major aid packages for Ukraine and Taiwan) and sanctions (anti on Iran‑related bills but interventionist on a 2025 sanctions bill). She has 8 breaking anti votes, but only one of those directly opposes her party on the Israel anchor, and she has not signed any discharge petitions against her own leadership. No lobby money from the Israel lobby is reported, but the lack of strong defections and the inconsistent Israel votes lower confidence. Overall she appears more aligned with party leadership than a reliable anti‑establishment ally.
BG:K000400.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she has voted inconsistently on aid to Israel, including supporting a major Israel military aid package, and lacks strong anti‑establishment defection evidence.

Sánchez serves on the Ways and Means Committee; she was the ranking member on the House Ethics Committee until 2017. In the 114th Congress, she chaired the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

BG:S001156.tier_writeup: Linda Sanchez is a sitting Democratic representative from California who is retiring in 2026. While she has cast several votes against military aid and for the repeal of war authorizations, her record is fundamentally inconsistent on the coalition's anchor issue: aid to the State of Israel. Specifically, she has voted against supplemental security assistance to Israel (H R 7217, H R 8369) but later voted in favor of a supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel (H R 8034). Her record on military aid to other countries and sanctions is also inconsistent, frequently voting with her party on interventionist measures such as the Ukraine Support Act and various sanctions. Although she has broken with her party on specific use-of-force resolutions, her inability to hold a principled line on Israel prevents her from being a reliable ally. She does not actively back a specific party leader in the provided data, but her voting patterns suggest she follows the party majority on most high-stakes interventionist bills.
BG:S001156.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she has failed to maintain a consistent anti-interventionist record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel.

BG:T000472.tier_writeup: Mark Takano is a sitting Democrat from California with a mixed record on foreign intervention. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, he is inconsistent, having voted against supplemental aid in 2024 but voting for an amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security in 2025, which is an interventionist position. His record on military aid to other countries is also inconsistent, with anti-interventionist votes on cluster munitions in 2023 but interventionist votes on the PROTECT Taiwan Act and Ukraine Support Act in 2026. He has shown some principle in voting against war authorizations and for removing forces from unauthorized hostilities, but these are often party-line votes or non-binding resolutions. He has signed discharge petitions, but the facts indicate zero applicable discharge petitions were signed against his own leadership. His donor record is clean of Israel lobby money, but his voting record does not hold the line on the core anti-interventionist principles, particularly regarding Israel and recent arms transfers.

BG:K000397.tier_writeup: Young Kim is a reliable establishment vote whose record is overwhelmingly interventionist across all five tracked areas. She fails the coalition's anchor test, having consistently voted to provide supplemental security assistance to Israel (H.R. 7217, H.R. 8034) and against amendments to strike or prohibit such funding (H.R. 4016, H.R. 8595). Her record on the use of force is equally rigid; she has voted against every recent resolution to remove U.S. armed forces from foreign conflicts, including measures concerning Syria, Somalia, and Yemen. While she occasionally breaks from her party on specific arms sales—notably opposing F-16 transfers to Turkey in 2022 and a specific Ukraine aid package in 2026—these are outliers in a career defined by supporting military aid to Taiwan, Lebanon, and Ukraine. She further demonstrated her establishment alignment by voting against the repeal of the 1991 and 2002 authorizations for use of military force. Given her consistent support for the Israel lobby and her 96% party-loyalty rate, her rare anti-interventionist votes appear to be isolated policy disagreements rather than a shift in principle.
BG:K000397.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she consistently supports military aid to Israel and has voted against nearly every effort to restrain the U.S. use of force abroad.

BG:G000598.tier_writeup: Robert Garcia is a sitting Democrat from California who has shown a mixed record on foreign intervention. While he has consistently voted against broad war authorizations and for restraining U.S. use of force abroad, his record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with only 3 of 5 votes being anti-interventionist. Notably, he voted for supplemental security assistance to Israel in 2024 and voted against an amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security in 2025, which are interventionist positions. His record on military aid to other countries is also inconsistent, with 3 of 23 votes being anti-interventionist, including votes against prohibiting cluster munitions to Ukraine. Although he has signed discharge petitions and cosponsored bills limiting arms transfers to Israel, his recent votes on Israel aid and military assistance to Ukraine and Lebanon suggest he is not a reliable anti-establishment ally. His lack of significant lobbying money from the Israel lobby is a positive sign, but his voting record does not support a hard tier.
BG:G000598.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with recent interventionist votes that undermine his anti-interventionist stance.

BG:W000187.tier_writeup: Maxine Waters is a sitting Democrat from California with a long history of anti-war rhetoric, but her voting record fails the anchor test for reliability. On aid to Israel, she is inconsistent, having voted against supplemental aid in 2024 but then voting with the establishment to block amendments striking Israeli funding in 2025. Her record on military aid to other countries is largely interventionist, as she voted against amendments prohibiting aid to Ukraine, Lebanon, and Taiwan in 2024, 2025, and 2026. While she has voted against war authorizations and for resolutions to remove troops from hostilities, these votes often aligned with her party majority or were non-binding. She has signed discharge petitions, but none were against her own party's leadership, which is a key indicator of principled defiance. Her lack of consistency on the anchor issue of Israel aid, combined with her failure to break with her party on major military aid bills, marks her as a partisan rather than a reliable anti-establishment ally.

BG:M001241.tier_writeup: Dave Min is a sitting Democrat from California who previously served in the state senate. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, his record is inconsistent; he voted with the interventionist majority in July 2025 but broke with his party in July 2026 to support an amendment prohibiting funds for Israel. This recent anti-interventionist vote is a positive signal, but it is not yet a consistent pattern, as he has only one anti vote in this area. In the area of use of force abroad, he has been consistently anti-interventionist, voting against resolutions that would have authorized or continued military actions. He has also consistently voted against broad war authorizations, including repealing the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs. However, his record on military aid to other countries is mixed; he voted against amendments to strike aid to Ukraine and Taiwan in 2025, but voted for the PROTECT Taiwan Act and the Ukraine Support Act in 2026. He has signed discharge petitions, but none are applicable to the specific anti-interventionist measures currently blocked by leadership. His donors include pro-Israel groups that targeted him in the 2024 primary, which suggests he is under pressure from the establishment on this issue. While his recent votes show a shift toward anti-interventionism, the lack of consistency on the anchor issue and the mixed record on military aid to other countries prevent him from being counted as a reliable ally.
BG:M001241.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record is inconsistent on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, showing a recent turn that has not yet been sustained, and he lacks the sustained leadership defiance required for a hard ally.

BG:I000056.description: Darrell Edward Issa is an American businessman and politician serving as the U.S. representative for California's 48th congressional district. He represented the 50th congressional district from 2021 to 2023. A member of the Republican Party, he previously served in the United States House of Representatives from 2001 to 2019, representing two districts primarily covering North County in the San Diego area: first the 48th district for one term and then the 49th district for eight terms. From January 2011 to January 2015, he chaired the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

BG:J000305.tier_writeup: Sara Jacobs is a sitting Democrat from California who has cast numerous anti-interventionist votes, particularly regarding the use of force abroad and war authorizations. However, her record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, as she voted against supplemental security assistance in 2024 but voted for a supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel in April 2024. In July 2025, she voted against an amendment to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security, which is an interventionist vote on the anchor issue. While she has broken with her party on other issues, such as repealing the 2002 AUMF and directing the removal of forces from unauthorized hostilities, the failure to maintain a consistent anti-interventionist stance on aid to Israel disqualifies her from being a reliable ally. Her recent votes in 2026 show continued support for removing forces from Lebanon and other areas, but the earlier interventionist votes on Israel aid remain a significant barrier to trust. The record shows a mix of principled anti-war stances and party-line votes on critical aid packages, suggesting a lack of the consistency required for a hard tier.
BG:J000305.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because her record on aid to Israel is inconsistent, including votes for military aid to Israel in 2024 and 2025 that break the anchor requirement.

BG:V000130.tier_writeup: Juan Vargas is a Democratic incumbent from California who has a mixed and inconsistent foreign policy record. While he has occasionally broken with his party on issues regarding the use of force and certain military aid votes, he fails the most critical test of reliability: consistency on aid to the State of Israel. His record on the anchor issue is highly inconsistent, having voted for supplemental security assistance to Israel in early 2024 (H R 7217) and later voting for a motion to recommit on the Israel Security Assistance Support Act (H R 8369). Furthermore, his cosponsorship of resolutions condemning Hamas (HRES 839) and recognizing the October 7 attacks (HRES 1618) signals a alignment with interventionist frameworks. His votes on military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan have also trended toward the establishment in the 119th Congress. Because he has not held a consistent anti-interventionist line on Israel, he cannot be considered a reliable ally.

Across foreign military aid to other nations, she voted interventionist on 25 of 31 votes, consistently backing aid packages and funding for Ukraine and Taiwan. Her anti-interventionist votes primarily occurred on non-binding measures or use of force resolutions when aligned with party leadership, defecting to the anti-interventionist side on just 7 of 76 focus votes. She signed no discharge petitions against her own party's leadership. Ultimately, her voting record reflects party-line establishment positioning rather than anti-interventionist principle.

BG:C001121.tier_writeup: Jason Crow is a sitting Democrat from Colorado with a military background, but his voting record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with only 3 of 5 votes aligning with the anti-interventionist position. While he voted against the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in 2024, he voted in favor of a supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel in April 2024, demonstrating a lack of consistency on the primary metric. His record on other areas is mixed; he has voted against broad war authorizations and supported resolutions to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, but he has also voted for military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan, which are considered interventionist under the coalition's criteria. Crow has signed discharge petitions, but the facts indicate these were not against his own party's leadership, limiting their weight as evidence of principled defiance. He has received campaign donations from Palantir Technologies, a company that provides services to the IDF, which raises concerns about his independence from interests that profit from the status quo. Although he recently voted for an amendment to eliminate regular aid to Israel in 2026, the prior inconsistency in 2024 prevents him from being classified as a reliable ally. His overall record suggests a member who is shifting toward anti-interventionist positions but has not yet established the consistent, principled track record required for a hard tier.
BG:C001121.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, failing to meet the reliability standard for a hard ally.

BG:P000620.tier_writeup: Brittany Pettersen is a sitting Democratic member from Colorado's 7th district, first casting an anti-interventionist vote on 2024-02-06, and her record is genuinely mixed rather than empty. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel she is inconsistent: she voted Nay on HR 7217 (2024-02-06) and Nay on HR 8369 (2024-05-16) but Yea on the HR 8034 supplemental (2024-04-20), and in the 119th she split again, voting Nay on the Greene amendment to strike Israel cooperative funding (2025-07-18) and Yea on the HR 8595 amendment (2026-07-15) with only 48 percent of her own party, which is her one real own-party defection on the anchor. On military aid to other countries she has been consistently interventionist, voting Nay on amendments to bar funding for Ukraine, Lebanon and Taiwan in 2024, 2025 and 2026, and Yea on the Ukraine Support Act (HR 2913, 2026-06-04) with 98 percent of her party. On sanctions she is turning rather than settled: Yea on HR 1998 (2025-06-23) with 97 percent of her party, with the dossier showing her consistent against measures touching Ansarallah and turning on Iran. Her strongest area is war authorizations and use of force, where she is 3 of 3 against authorizations and has repeatedly voted to direct the removal of U.S. forces (H CON RES 64, 61, 68, 38, 75, 86, 108, 89, 93), including the 2025-09-10 amendment repealing the 1991 and 2002 Iraq AUMFs, though she also voted Nay on H CON RES 84 (2026-06-04) with only 57 percent of her party. She has signed discharge petitions (H.Res. 278, 391, 393) but all signers were from her own party and the dossier shows zero petitions against her own leadership, so she has not gone around her Speaker or Rules Committee. On money, the dossier shows no TrackAIPAC contributions, no AIPAC endorsement or approval, and no outside spending for or against her, which is clean but also gives no counter-signal. The news items show she was targeted by AIPAC-aligned spending after voting against Israel aid and that she missed a Hegseth impeachment vote while attending an event, which cuts both ways on reliability. Overall this is a member whose anti-war votes are real and repeated but whose support for Ukraine and other arms transfers, plus her flip on the 2024 supplemental, keeps her below the floor for a hard verdict.

BG:L000557.tier_writeup: John Larson is a long-serving Democratic representative from Connecticut who was defeated in the 2026 primary. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, with only two anti-interventionist votes out of five counted, including a recent interventionist vote in July 2026. While he has voted against broad war authorizations and for removing troops from unauthorized hostilities, these votes largely align with the Democratic party majority rather than representing a principled break. He has only one recorded breaking anti-interventionist vote, which is insufficient to establish reliability. His votes on military aid to other countries and sanctions are also inconsistent or interventionist, such as supporting the PROTECT Taiwan Act and Ukraine Support Act. There is no evidence of significant lobbying money from the Israel lobby, but his voting pattern suggests partisanship over principle. He does not meet the floor for a reliable anti-establishment ally due to the lack of consistency on the anchor issue and the absence of meaningful own-party defections.

BG:C001069.tier_writeup: Joe Courtney is a sitting Democrat from Connecticut who has served in the House since 2011. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent, as he voted against supplemental security assistance in 2024 but voted for a supplemental appropriations bill providing military aid to Israel in April 2024. He also voted against an amendment in 2025 that sought to strike funding for Israeli Cooperative Security and against an amendment in 2026 to prohibit funds from being used for certain Israeli purposes. While he has voted against broad war authorizations and for resolutions directing the removal of U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran, these votes align with the majority of his own party and do not demonstrate independent principle. He has no breaking votes against his own party on the anchor issue of aid to Israel, and his anti-interventionist votes on other issues are largely party-line. The lack of consistency on the anchor issue disqualifies him from being a reliable anti-establishment ally, regardless of his other votes.

He has cast only one breaking anti-interventionist vote in his career, which was on a war authorization repeal, and has never voted against his own party on aid to Israel. His record on military aid to other countries is consistently interventionist, as he voted against amendments to prohibit aid to Ukraine, Lebanon, and Taiwan. While he has voted against broad war authorizations and for resolutions to remove U.S. forces from various conflicts, these votes were largely cast with his own party majority. He has signed discharge petitions, but none were applicable to blocking anti-interventionist measures or defying his own leadership in a way that signals principle over partisanship. His financial record shows heavy reliance on large donors and PACs, with no specific evidence of Israel lobby money, but the lack of principled defections on the anchor issue is disqualifying. He is viewed as a standard establishment Democrat who votes with his party on foreign policy, rather than a reliable anti-establishment ally.

Her record on use of force abroad is consistent, with 11 of 14 votes against restraining U.S. use of force, including recent votes to direct the removal of forces from Lebanon and Iran. She has signed multiple discharge petitions, though the facts do not specify if these were against her own leadership. Her lack of consistency on the Israel aid anchor issue, combined with recent interventionist votes on military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan, prevents her from being classified as a reliable anti-establishment ally.

BG:D000628.tier_writeup: Neal Dunn is a sitting Republican Representative from Florida who has repeatedly voted to provide military aid to Israel, including Yea votes on the 2024 supplemental security assistance bill, the 2024 Israel Security Assistance Support Act, and the 2026 amendment to prohibit Israel funding. He has no anti‑Israel votes and no breaking anti‑interventionist votes on that anchor issue. His record on the other four criteria is mixed but overwhelmingly interventionist: only 2 of 30 military‑aid votes were anti, and his anti votes on Ukraine and Lebanon were isolated and often aligned with a minority of his party. He has not signed any discharge petitions against his own leadership, nor has he publicly defied party leaders. Lobby‑money data shows no direct AIPAC contributions, but his overall alignment with the Republican establishment and consistent support for foreign military aid make him unreliable. Consequently, he should be treated as an establishment figure, not a dependable anti‑establishment ally.
BG:D000628.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently supports Israel aid and has a largely interventionist voting record with no meaningful anti‑interventionist breaking votes.

BG:C001039.tier_writeup: Kat Cammack is a sitting Republican representative from Florida who has cast numerous anti-interventionist votes on military aid to Ukraine, Lebanon, and NATO, often breaking with her own party. However, her record fails the critical anchor test regarding aid to the State of Israel, as she voted in favor of supplemental security assistance and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in 2024. While she has shown consistency in opposing military aid to other countries like Ukraine and Lebanon, her support for Israel aligns her with the establishment position on the most significant foreign policy issue for this coalition. Her votes on use of force and war authorizations are inconsistent, with recent interventionist votes on concurrent resolutions directing the President. There is no evidence of her signing discharge petitions or actively defying leadership on procedural matters to advance anti-interventionist goals. Her voting pattern suggests a mix of genuine skepticism toward certain foreign entanglements and strong partisan loyalty on issues where her party and the Israel lobby are aligned. Consequently, she cannot be counted on as a reliable ally for a coalition that prioritizes anti-interventionism across all five areas, particularly given her failure on the anchor issue.

BG:B001314.tier_writeup: Representative Aaron Bean is a sitting House member from Florida who fails to meet the coalition threshold for anti-interventionism. On the anchor issue of aid to the State of Israel, Bean voted anti-interventionist once on H R 7217 in February 2024, but subsequently reversed course by voting for Israeli military aid on H R 8034 in April 2024 and against restricting Israeli funding on H R 8595 in July 2026. While he accumulated 22 anti-interventionist votes opposing arms aid and assistance to Ukraine and NATO, his record on the use of force abroad is heavily interventionist. In June 2026, Bean voted against H CON RES 86 and H CON RES 84, rejecting war powers limitations on military involvement abroad and supporting military actions regarding Iran. He has signed zero discharge petitions against party leadership and shows a voting pattern that aligns with political positioning rather than sustained non-interventionist principle. Consequently, Bean cannot be counted on as a reliable anti-establishment ally.
BG:B001314.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he failed to remain consistent on aid to Israel and repeatedly voted for military intervention and open-ended use of force abroad.

BG:M001216.tier_writeup: Cory Mills is a sitting Republican representative from Florida who has been defeated in the 2026 primary. His record on the anchor issue of aid to Israel is inconsistent and ultimately interventionist; while he voted against supplemental aid in early 2024, he voted for the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in May 2024 and voted against amendments to prohibit Israeli aid in 2025 and 2026. This failure to hold an anti-interventionist line on Israel disqualifies him from being a reliable ally, regardless of his other votes. In the area of military aid to other countries, he has been consistently anti-interventionist, voting against aid to Ukraine, Lebanon, and NATO, often breaking with his party. He also voted to repeal the 1991 and 2002 Authorizations for Use of Military Force, which is a strong anti-interventionist signal. BG:F000476.tier_writeup: Maxwell Frost (D‑FL‑10) is a sitting member who has voted anti on several interventionist measures, including use‑of‑force resolutions and some war‑authorization amendments, and he has broken with his own party on at least ten occasions. However, his record on the anchor issue—aid to Israel—is inconsistent: he voted against aid in four of five relevant bills and has not maintained a steady anti stance, including a 2025 vote supporting an amendment that would have struck Israeli‑cooperation funding. He also shows mixed consistency on military aid to other countries and sanctions, with anti votes on some items (e.g., cluster‑munitions amendments) but later interventionist votes on Ukraine, Taiwan, and other aid packages. Frost has signed discharge petitions (e.g., H.Res. 250, H.Res. 278, H.Res. 432) but none directly target his own leadership on interventionist measures. He reports no contributions from the Israel lobby or war‑industry donors, suggesting low capital risk. While he demonstrates genuine anti‑intervention sentiment on many issues, the inconsistency on aid to Israel and the broader pattern of shifting positions indicate mixed principle versus partisan positioning, making him an unreliable anti‑establishment ally.

Thus his anti‑interventionist signals are outweighed by clear interventionist behavior on the anchor issue, making him unreliable for the coalition.

While he has cast a handful of anti‑intervention votes, his record on the anchor issue—aid to Israel—is clearly interventionist, voting Yea on multiple Israel security assistance bills in 2024 and 2025 and only one Nay that was procedural. This inconsistency on the anchor area disqualifies him as a reliable anti‑establishment ally. He has some anti‑votes on military aid to other countries and use of force, but these are sporadic and often overridden by party majorities, showing no principled break. He has not signed any discharge petitions against his party leadership, and there is no evidence of active backing of an establishment leader, but the anchor failure alone is decisive. Money from the Israel lobby is not listed, yet his voting pattern aligns with pro‑Israel positions. Overall, his anti‑votes appear limited and likely tactical rather than principled.

BG:S001214.tier_writeup: W. Steube is a sitting Republican Representative from Florida's 17th district. While he has broken with his party on 29 foreign‑policy votes, his record on aid to Israel is clearly interventionist, voting Yea on three separate Israel security assistance bills in 2024 and a 2025 amendment to strike funding for Israeli cooperation. The anchor rule requires a reliable anti‑interventionist to be consistently anti‑Israel, which Steube is not. His military‑aid votes to other countries are mixed, and he has voted both anti and pro on use‑of‑force resolutions and war authorizations, showing inconsistency. He has signed a few discharge petitions, but none target his own leadership on the Israel issue. No lobby money from AIPAC is reported, but his voting pattern outweighs donor considerations. Overall his anti‑intervention votes appear selective and partisan rather than principled, making him unreliable under pressure.
BG:S001214.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel, violating the anchor anti‑intervention rule.

BG:F000472.tier_writeup: Rep. Scott Franklin (R‑FL) has a mixed foreign‑policy record but fails the anchor test on Israel. He voted Yea on three separate Israel security assistance bills in 2024 and again supported Israel‑related funding in 2025, aligning with his party 94‑100% of the time. His anti‑interventionist votes are limited to a handful of amendments on NATO, Ukraine and Lebanon, and he has only nine defections overall, many of which are procedural or on narrow funding cuts. He has not signed any discharge petitions against his leadership and receives no documented lobby money from the Israel lobby, but his consistent pro‑Israel voting outweighs any occasional anti‑aid votes. The pattern shows partisan alignment rather than principled anti‑interventionism, making him unreliable for the coalition.
BG:F000472.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record on aid to Israel is consistently interventionist and he lacks reliable anti‑establishment breaking votes.

BG:D000032.description: Byron Lowell Donalds is an American politician who is the governor-elect of Florida. Donalds has served as the U.S. representative for Florida's 19th congressional district since 2021. His congressional district includes much of Southwest Florida. From 2016 to 2020, he served in the Florida House of Representatives. A member of the Republican Party, Donalds was elected governor of Florida in the 2026 Florida gubernatorial election, becoming the first African American elected to the position.

BG:D000032.tier_screen: breaks from own party toward the anti side on 25 foreign-policy votes
BG:D000032.tier_writeup: Byron Donalds is a sitting Republican from Florida who is retiring in 2026. While he has cast 25 breaking votes against his party on foreign policy, primarily opposing aid to Ukraine and repealing war authorizations, he fails the critical anchor test regarding aid to Israel. In 2024, he voted in favor of supplemental security assistance to Israel (H R 7217) and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act (H R 8369), and in 2026, he voted against an amendment to prohibit funds for Israeli Cooperative Security (H R 4016). His public statements explicitly support standing behind Israel 100% and he has endorsed the 2026 Iran War, describing it as a necessary action to prevent nuclear proliferation. Although he opposes Ukraine aid, his consistent support for Israel's military and his hawkish stance on Iran and Cuba regime change demonstrate that his anti-interventionism is selective and aligned with pro-Israel establishment positions rather than a principled opposition to foreign intervention. Therefore, he cannot be counted as a reliable anti-establishment ally.
BG:D000032.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he voted for military aid to Israel in 2024 and 2026, failing the anchor requirement for a reliable anti-interventionist ally.

BG:M001199.tier_screen: breaks from own party toward the anti side on 13 foreign-policy votes
BG:M001199.tier_writeup: Brian Mast is a sitting Republican from Florida who has voted against a handful of foreign‑policy measures that could be seen as anti‑interventionist, but his record on aid to Israel is firmly interventionist. He voted for multiple supplemental appropriations bills that provide security assistance to Israel, and he has not broken with his party on that anchor issue. While he has cast a few anti‑aid votes on Ukraine and other countries, those votes are inconsistent and do not demonstrate a principled stance. He has not signed any discharge petitions against his own leadership, and there is no evidence of active opposition to the current Speaker or party leadership. With no clear pattern of principled defiance and a lack of consistent anti‑Israel voting, he does not meet the criteria for a reliable anti‑establishment ally.
BG:M001199.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because his record shows no consistent anti‑Israel aid stance and his anti‑intervention votes are limited and largely procedural.

BG:F000462.tier_writeup: Lois Frankel is a retiring Democratic representative with a long career in Florida and national politics that reflects a standard establishment foreign policy. Her record on the coalition's anchor issue is disqualifying: she has consistently voted for military aid to the State of Israel, including supplemental packages in 2024 and 2026, and has opposed efforts to strike that funding. Beyond Israel, she has regularly supported military aid to Ukraine and Taiwan while voting against amendments to restrict such assistance. While she has voted to repeal outdated war authorizations and supported some resolutions to remove U.S. troops from foreign conflicts, these votes almost always occurred alongside the vast majority of her party and do not represent a break from leadership. With zero breaking anti-interventionist votes and a history of cosponsoring pro-intervention legislation, she remains firmly within the establishment camp.
BG:F000462.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she has consistently voted to provide military aid to the State of Israel and other foreign nations, maintaining a record that aligns with the establishment on nearly every major interventionist vote.

BG:W000797.tier_writeup: Debbie Wasserman Schultz is a sitting Democrat from Florida who has served in Congress since 2012. Her record on aid to Israel is inconsistent and ultimately interventionist, as she voted Yea on H R 7217 in 2024 and Nay on the Greene amendment to strike Israeli funding in 2025. Although she voted Nay on the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in 2024, this single anti-vote is outweighed by her consistent support for military aid to other countries, including Ukraine and Taiwan. She voted Yea on the Ukraine Support Act and the PROTECT Taiwan Act in 2026, demonstrating a strong pro-intervention stance on global conflicts. Her record on war authorizations is anti-interventionist, as she voted to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, but this does not offset her support for active military aid. She has no breaking votes against her own party on the anchor issue of Israel aid, and her anti-votes on use of force are largely party-line votes. The record shows a member who supports the establishment foreign policy consensus on aid and arms, making her unreliable as an anti-establishment ally.
BG:W000797.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because she voted for aid to Israel in 2024 and 2025, failing the anchor requirement for reliability.

BG:D000600.tier_writeup: Mario Diaz-Balart is a Republican incumbent representing Florida's 26th Congressional District. Across 75 focus votes on arms, aid, and war, he voted anti-interventionist only 4 times, maintaining an overwhelmingly interventionist record. On the anchor area of aid to Israel, he has never taken an anti-interventionist stance, consistently voting for assistance packages such as H.R. 7217, H.R. 8034, and H.R. 8369, while voting against amendments to prohibit funding. His supporting record is similarly interventionist, marked by frequent votes against War Powers resolutions seeking to remove U.S. armed forces abroad and votes sustaining military aid to countries such as Taiwan and Ukraine. While he cast two breaking votes opposing military aid—specifically on Turkey F-16 sales in H.R. 7900 and on H.R. 2913—these isolated votes represent no broader anti-interventionist shift. TrackAIPAC records show zero tracked contributions or outside spending for or against him. He remains an entrenched establishment legislator who cannot be counted on when intervention votes matter.
BG:D000600.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes in favor of aid to Israel and reliably backs foreign military aid, sanctions, and foreign interventions.

BG:J000311.tier_writeup: Brian Jack is a sitting Republican from Georgia who has voted against a handful of foreign‑policy measures, but none of those votes concern aid to Israel, the anchor issue for our coalition. His record shows four anti‑intervention votes in the 119th Congress, all on military aid to other countries, but he has consistently supported U.S. aid to Israel and has not opposed any Israel‑related legislation. He has no evidence of signing discharge petitions against his own leadership, and his campaign contributions show no significant money from the Israel lobby. While he has broken with his party on a few votes, the lack of a breaking vote on aid to Israel and the overall inconsistency in his foreign‑policy positions mean he cannot be counted as a reliable ally. He is therefore classified as a soft signal, not a hard one.
BG:J000311.tier_bottom_line: Does not count as a reliable anti-establishment ally because he has not broken with his party on aid to Israel and his anti‑intervention record is inconsistent.

BG:J000288.tier_writeup: Henry Johnson is a sitting Democrat from Georgia who has shown some anti-interventionist tendencies but lacks the consistency required to be a reliable ally. On the anchor issue of aid to Israel, his record is inconsistent, with 4 of 5 votes anti-interventionist, including a notable break with his party on H.R. 8034 in 2024, but he voted interventionist on H.R. 4016 in 2025. His record on military aid to other countries is consistently interventionist, with only 1 of 30 votes anti, and he voted for the PROTECT Taiwan Act and Ukraine Support Act. On sanctions, his record is inconsistent, with 5 of 19 votes anti, including a break with his party on H.R. 3033 in 2024, but he voted for sanctions on Iran in 2025. He has been consistently anti-interventionist on use of force abroad and war authorizations, with 12 of 15 and 4 of 4 votes respectively, including breaking with his party on repealing the 2002 AUMF. He has signed discharge petitions but none against his own leadership. His record shows a mix of principled stands and party-line votes, making him a soft ally at best.

Williams served as one of 16 electors for Georgia in the Electoral College following the 2020 United States presidential election.

BG:S001189.tier_writeup: Austin Scott is a reliable establishment vote on foreign policy and military intervention. On the anchor issue of aid to the State of Israel, Scott has consistently voted for supplemental funding and against any measures to strike or prohibit such aid, even cosponsoring the Israel Security Assistance Support Act. His record on the use of force is equally interventionist; he has voted against numerous resolutions to remove U.S. troops from foreign conflicts and opposed the repeal of the 1991 and 2002 war authorizations. While he cast two isolated breaking votes—one against cluster munitions and one against a Ukraine aid package—these are outliers in a record otherwise defined by support for military aid to Taiwan, Ukraine, and Lebanon. Scott’s active cosponsorship of sanctions and his vocal support for maintaining military capabilities at Robins Air Force Base further align him with the defense establishment. He cannot be counted on by the coalition.
BG:S001189.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he is a consistent supporter of military aid to Israel and has repeatedly voted against restraining the use of U.S. force abroad.

BG:C001129.tier_writeup: Mike Collins is a sitting Republican from Georgia who is retiring in 2026. His record on the anchor issue of aid to the State of Israel is consistently interventionist, as he voted in favor of supplemental security assistance and the Israel Security Assistance Support Act in 2024 and 2025. Although he has cast 24 breaking votes against his own party on military aid to other countries such as Ukraine and Lebanon, these votes do not offset his pro-Israel stance. Public statements and campaign coverage confirm his strong support for Israel, including a 2026 C-SPAN interview where he cited his faith as a reason to support Israel in contrast to his opponent. He has not signed any discharge petitions to bypass party leadership on foreign policy measures. His voting pattern suggests that his anti-interventionist votes on other countries are likely driven by partisan alignment with the current administration's shifting priorities rather than a principled anti-interventionist worldview. Consequently, he cannot be relied upon to oppose interventionist policies when they align with his core pro-Israel commitments.
BG:C001129.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he has consistently voted for aid to the State of Israel, failing the anchor requirement for a reliable anti-interventionist ally.

BG:L000583.tier_writeup: Barry Loudermilk is a retiring Republican representative whose record is firmly establishment on foreign policy. He has consistently supported military aid to the State of Israel, voting for multiple supplemental packages and against amendments to strike that funding. While he has cast occasional votes against NATO funding and cluster munition transfers, these are outweighed by his consistent opposition to restraining the U.S. use of force; he repeatedly voted against resolutions to withdraw troops from foreign conflicts and against the repeal of outdated war authorizations. His record on military aid to other countries is inconsistent, supporting aid to Taiwan and occasionally Ukraine while opposing it for Lebanon. Ultimately, his adherence to the interventionist consensus on Israel and executive war powers makes him an unreliable ally for the coalition.
BG:L000583.tier_bottom_line: Does not count because he consistently votes for military aid to Israel and against measures to restrain the U.S. use of force abroad.
